title: He Has Risen: The Great Commission
summary: At dawn on the first day of the week, two women named Mary come to the tomb, and an angel rolls back the stone and tells them that Jesus has risen. Jesus himself meets them, and they worship him. The guards report to the chief priests, who pay them to say the disciples stole the body. On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus meets the eleven and sends them to make disciples of all nations, promising to be with them always.
story: The sealed and guarded tomb of 27:66 is where this chapter begins, and it ends the whole Gospel. Three times Jesus predicted that he would be killed and raised on the third day (16:21, 17:23, 20:19), and here the prediction is fulfilled. The chapter also resolves threads that run through the book: Jesus promised in 26:32 to go ahead of the disciples into Galilee, where his ministry began; the Gentile magi at the start find their answer in the command to disciple all nations; and the name Immanuel, God with us (1:23), is echoed in the Gospel's last promise, I am with you always. Matthew stops here, and the story continues in the life of the church, as Acts and the letters show.
historical:
The resurrection is the event on which the Christian faith stands or falls, and its historical evidence has been examined closely by believers and skeptics alike. Several facts are widely accepted by historians of many views. Jesus was crucified and buried. His followers, soon afterward, sincerely proclaimed that he had been raised bodily and that they had seen him. The earliest written witness is not a Gospel but a list of appearances that Paul says he received and passed on (1 Corinthians 15:3-8), which many scholars date to within a few years of the crucifixion; it names Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred people at once, James the brother of Jesus (previously not a follower), and Paul himself, a former persecutor. The movement began in Jerusalem, where the tomb's location was known, and the counter-claim reported in this chapter, that the disciples stole the body, implicitly concedes that the tomb was empty. The Christian writer Justin Martyr, in the second century, says that Jewish opponents in his day were still telling the same story.

The Gospels agree that women were the first witnesses. In the first century a woman's testimony was given less weight than a man's in many legal settings, and Josephus reports that it was not accepted in Jewish courts, so few would have invented women as the founding witnesses of a story they wanted believed. Skeptical scholars have proposed other explanations: theft of the body, visits to the wrong tomb, visionary experiences, or legend growing over time. Defenders respond that none of these explains both the empty tomb and the appearances to individuals and groups, including former skeptics, or the willingness of the witnesses to suffer for their claim. History can weigh such evidence, but it cannot compel faith; the church's confession, stated in every creed, is that Jesus was raised bodily from the dead on the third day. This is a first-order article of Christian faith, not an optional interpretation.
cultural:
Jews in the first century who believed in resurrection generally expected it at the end of the age, when all the righteous would be raised together (Daniel 12:2). No one expected one man to be raised in the middle of history ahead of everyone else, which is part of why the disciples were slow to believe and why their claim was so startling. The Sabbath ran from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, so the women came at the first opportunity after the day of rest, and in the other Gospels they bring spices to finish the burial rites.

Grasping someone's feet was a gesture of homage, and it also shows that the risen Jesus is touchable, not a ghost. Bribing soldiers to give false testimony was a familiar abuse, and Roman soldiers who fell asleep on duty could face severe punishment, which is why the leaders promise to satisfy the governor. The command to baptize reflects a practice already known from John the Baptist and from Jewish ritual washings, now performed in a single name shared by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
literary: The chapter is brief and built on two scenes of commissioning with a counter-scene between them. First the angel and then Jesus tell the women to go and tell. In the middle, the guards and chief priests invent their story, a deliberate contrast between true witness and bought testimony. Then Jesus commissions the eleven. The final scene echoes the end of the Old Testament as it was arranged in the Hebrew Bible, where Cyrus says that the Lord has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and appointed him to build the Lord's house, and he sends God's people up with the words may the Lord his God be with him (2 Chronicles 36:23). Matthew's ending also gathers the Gospel's key words: authority, all nations, teaching, commandments, and God with us. The note that some doubted (verse 17) is left honestly in the text.

outline.t: The empty tomb and the angel's message
The risen Jesus meets the women
The guards bribed to spread a false report

doctrines.note: The bodily resurrection of Jesus is the church's first-order confession and the ground of Christian hope. He was raised in the same body that was crucified and buried, now glorified, the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to his people.

Disciples are baptized into the one name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The singular name with three persons became one of the chief scriptural foundations for the church's confession of the Trinity.

The risen Jesus sends his followers to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them to obey all he commanded. Mission rests on his authority and is sustained by his presence to the end of the age.

Baptism is commanded by the risen Lord as the mark of entry into discipleship. Christians differ on whether it is given to infants of believers or only to those who profess faith, but all traditions trace the practice to this command.

words.note: Egeiro, to raise or rise, used of waking from sleep and of rising from the dead. The angel's announcement uses it twice. The passive form, he has been raised, points to God as the one who raised him, which is how the apostles preached it (Acts 2:24).

Matheteuo, to make disciples. It is the one command in the commission; going, baptizing, and teaching describe how it is done. A disciple is a learner and follower, so the task is not only to win converts but to form people who obey Jesus.

Distazo, to doubt or waver, used elsewhere in Matthew only of Peter sinking in the waves (14:31). That some doubted even while worshiping the risen Jesus is recorded without embarrassment, and Jesus comes near to them and commissions them all.

Exousia, authority. Jesus taught with authority and was challenged about it in the temple (21:23). Now he claims all authority in heaven and on earth, echoing Daniel 7:14, where the Son of Man receives dominion over all peoples.

christ: The chapter shows Christ risen, worshiped, and reigning. He is raised bodily, touchable, and recognizable, the firstfruits of the new creation. He accepts worship from the women and the disciples, which in Matthew belongs to God alone (4:10). He claims universal authority as Daniel's Son of Man, sends his people to all nations as God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed in his offspring, and places his own name beside the Father's and the Spirit's. And he promises his abiding presence, fulfilling the name Immanuel. The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is Lord, truly God and truly man, crucified and bodily risen, and present with his people until he comes again.

hard.q: Why do the resurrection accounts in the four Gospels differ in their details?
hard.a: Readers comparing the Gospels notice differences: how many women came and who they were, whether there was one angel or two, whether the first appearances were in Jerusalem or in Galilee, and in what order. Some see these as evidence that the stories grew as legend. Others point out that independent witnesses to a startling event usually differ in detail while agreeing on the core, and that deliberately invented accounts would more likely have been smoothed into agreement. Each Gospel also selects and arranges its material for its own purpose: Matthew, for example, focuses on Galilee and the commission to the nations, while Luke focuses on Jerusalem. Various harmonizations have been proposed, some more convincing than others. What all the accounts agree on is the heart of the matter: Jesus was buried, on the first day of the week women found the tomb empty, and the risen Jesus appeared to his followers, who were transformed by meeting him. That core is what the church confesses.

questions: The women left the tomb with fear and great joy at once. Why might both be the right response to the resurrection?
Some of the disciples worshiped and doubted on the same mountain, and Jesus sent them anyway. What does this say to people who carry doubts into their faith?
Jesus' last words promise his presence always. How would believing that change the way you approach the tasks and fears in front of you?
